THOUGHT: The patient has flaccid, easily ruptured blisters on the forearm with a positive Nikolsky sign and prominent mucosal involvement (oral and vulvar ulcers). Histopathology shows acantholysis with intraepidermal blister formation, and direct immunofluorescence demonstrates intercellular (net-like) IgG and C3 deposition within the epidermis. Serum autoantibodies to desmoglein are present. These clinical, histologic, immunopathologic, and serologic findings are classic for an antibody-mediated loss of keratinocyte cell–cell adhesion (desmoglein-targeted), i.e., pemphigus vulgaris. Differential diagnoses (bullous pemphigoid, Stevens–Johnson syndrome/TEN, erythema multiforme, paraneoplastic pemphigus) are less likely because bullous pemphigoid shows tense subepidermal blisters and linear basement membrane IgG/C3; SJS/TEN shows widespread epidermal necrosis rather than acantholysis; paraneoplastic pemphigus can have mixed findings and is associated with an underlying neoplasm (no such history here), and the presence of anti-desmoglein antibodies plus classic intraepidermal acantholysis strongly favors pemphigus vulgaris. Recent medication exposure (e.g., captopril) can sometimes trigger or exacerbate autoimmune blistering, but the underlying diagnosis remains pemphigus vulgaris.

DIAGNOSIS: Pemphigus vulgaris.
